newsitem.title: NORWAY: Holbrooke has no plans to return to U.S. govt.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke has no plans to return to U.S. govt.

text.p: Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. mediator who brokered the Dayton peace deal and then quit as Assistant Secretary of State, said on Thursday he had no plans to join the government again.
He said he did not want to think about reports that he had been nominated for the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize for negotiating the Bosnia peace agreement.

Holbrooke, in Oslo to address the Norwegian Nobel Foundation, has been mentioned as a possible successor to Secretary of State Warren Christopher should President Bill Clinton win the November 5 election.
"I have no career plans," Holbrooke told a news conference. "When I left the government the secretary of state and the president asked me to sign on as an unpaid consultant.

"They are in constant communication with me, as recently as last night they called, and I would do whatever they asked as a private citizen but I have no plans to return to the U.S. government," he said.
Holbrooke resigned in the afterglow of last year's Dayton peace treaty and went to Wall Street as an investment banker.
"I did not leave on policy grounds or financial grounds," he said. "I left for personal reasons."

Asked how he felt about being tipped as a possible winner of the peace prize, he replied: "I don't want to think about that. I heard rumours but I know nothing about it and it is not something one wants to think about."
Nobel sources have said Holbrooke and U.S. President Bill Clinton are among more than 100 candidates for this year's prize, awarded in October.
